problem:
Meridian Bank wants to connect its customers to instant payment systems in three markets: UPI in India, SCT Inst in Europe, and FedNow and RTP in the United States. Its engineers have shown that the technical connection is feasible, and its product team has assumed that a technical connection means the systems will behave the same way. That assumption breaks on the first cross-border payment, because the systems differ on the points that decide the customer promise: maximum amounts, execution windows, operating hours, confirmation rules and dispute processes.

The numbers make the point. SCT Inst has no scheme-level maximum and a 10-second maximum execution window. FedNow has a maximum of USD 10 million with a participant default of USD 100,000, and RTP has a limit of USD 10 million. UPI has a limit of INR 5 lakh for specified categories. The Indian rails operate 24x7x365, while other systems have their own operating models and cut-offs. A payment that is instant on one system and batched on another cannot be sold as instant end to end.

Meridian Bank needs an interoperability design that compares technical connectivity with scheme rule alignment, and that only promises what the slowest aligned rule permits. The design must also say what happens when the rules do not align, because that is the normal case, not the exception.
solution:
Assess interoperability on four layers and require alignment on each before a customer promise is made. Layer one is technical connectivity: message formats, APIs, identifiers and character sets. Layer two is scheme rules: maximum amounts, execution windows, finality, return and refund rights, and timeout behaviour. Layer three is operating model: operating hours, cut-offs, liquidity arrangements and settlement cycles. Layer four is dispute and exception handling: who investigates, what evidence is needed, and what the customer is owed when a leg fails.

Where the layers do not align, the corridor design must say so explicitly and choose a handling rule. If the limits differ, the corridor applies the lower effective limit for the corridor and discloses it before the customer confirms. If the execution windows differ, the end-to-end promise is the sum of the aligned windows plus FX and screening time, not the fastest leg. If the dispute processes differ, the corridor names a single investigation owner and a single customer SLA, and the participants agree the evidence each will supply.

The bridge between two domestic systems is an orchestration layer, not a passthrough. It translates data through a canonical model, enforces the corridor limits, binds the FX quote, runs the corridor screening, and holds the end-to-end state. It reports leg confirmations separately and only reports completion when the required confirmations arrive. A leg that is instant and a leg that is batched are both shown truthfully, so a customer who pays on a UPI leg that confirms in seconds and an onward leg that settles in a batch understands the journey before they pay.

decision.question: Meridian Bank plans a corridor between UPI in India and SCT Inst in Europe. The technical teams confirm both systems can exchange messages. The product team wants to advertise the corridor as instant end to end with a single 10-second promise. The learner must decide what promise the bank can honestly make.

options.label: A
options.detail: Drop the corridor because the two systems have different limits.

options.label: B
options.detail: Advertise a 10-second end-to-end promise, because SCT Inst executes in 10 seconds.

options.label: C
options.detail: Advertise the corridor as instant and handle any delay as a customer complaint.

options.label: D
options.detail: Promise only what the aligned rules permit: instant domestic legs with an end-to-end confirmation that depends on both legs, FX and screening, and publish the leg-level timings.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because interoperability requires alignment of scheme rules, limits, hours and dispute processes, not just technical connectivity, and the customer promise must reflect the slowest aligned rule. Option B is wrong because the SCT Inst window governs only the euro leg. Option C is wrong because it sells a promise the corridor cannot keep. Option A is wrong because different limits can be managed with routing and disclosure rather than by abandoning the corridor.

steps.title: Maps the scheme rules of each domestic system: limits, execution windows, hours, finality and dispute rules.
Designs the canonical model and the translation rules for identifiers, addresses and purpose codes.
Instructs a cross-border instant payment and sees the corridor limit and the expected leg timings before confirming.
Validates the instruction against the corridor limit and runs screening with synchronous decision deadlines.
Executes the domestic leg under its own scheme rules and returns its confirmation.
Revalidates the FX quote, checks liquidity, and instructs the destination domestic leg.
Executes the destination leg under its own scheme rules and returns its confirmation.
Matches both leg confirmations and publishes the end-to-end status with leg-level detail.

happy: The corridor is designed with aligned rules: the corridor limit is set at the lower effective limit, the end-to-end timing is published as the sum of the leg windows plus FX and screening, and a single investigation owner is named. A customer payment passes screening, the originating leg confirms, the bridge revalidates the FX quote, the destination leg confirms, and the customer sees a complete timeline with the time of each leg. Reconciliation matches both legs to the corridor settlement account without exception.

negative.title: Limit mismatch blocks the payment
negative.detail: The payment amount fits the originating system limit but exceeds the destination system limit. Block the payment before debit with a clear limit message, offer to split the payment only where the customer agrees and the scheme permits it, and never silently reduce the amount.

negative.title: Asynchronous legs with no destination confirmation
negative.detail: The originating leg confirms but the destination leg produces no confirmation within the corridor timeout. Enter the investigation state, keep the end-to-end status unconfirmed, and resolve through leg reconciliation before any retry or compensation.

negative.title: Dispute process mismatch
negative.detail: The two systems have different investigation evidence and timelines, so neither side accepts the other's evidence. Apply the corridor dispute agreement, with the named investigation owner collecting the agreed evidence set from both sides and owning the customer communication.

negative.title: Screening delay breaks the instant window
negative.detail: A mandatory check on one leg cannot complete inside that leg's processing window. Apply the fail-closed rule for that leg, hold the payment with a clear reason, and never release it to protect the corridor speed promise.

technical: Maintain a scheme rule register that records, for each domestic system, the maximum amount, the execution window, the operating hours, the finality rule, the return and refund rights, and the dispute process, with effective dates and a named owner for each entry. Build the canonical model to preserve the instruction ID, end-to-end ID and UETR where applicable, plus the structured or hybrid address and the purpose code, across the translation. Enforce the corridor limit as the lower effective limit of the aligned systems, and validate it before debit. Make every leg posting idempotent on its leg ID, keep leg states durable and separate from the orchestration state, and record the translation decisions so a field that cannot be mapped is flagged rather than dropped. Note the current figures in the register: SCT Inst has no scheme maximum and a 10-second window, FedNow has a maximum of USD 10 million with a participant default of USD 100,000, RTP has a limit of USD 10 million, and UPI has a limit of INR 5 lakh for specified categories.

accounting: Each domestic leg posts its own linked entries against a corridor settlement account, so the originating receipt, the FX conversion and the destination payout reconcile independently and in total. A leg that confirms without its counterpart is parked in a corridor suspense worklist owned by the bridge operator, and no compensation is posted until the leg states are established. Daily reconciliation covers the corridor settlement account, the FX execution account and the domestic leg control accounts, with same-day break ageing. Operations monitors limit breaches, leg timeouts, screening holds and dispute cases as separate queues, and the corridor limit and timing promise are reviewed whenever any participating scheme changes its rules, so a rule change on one side cannot silently invalidate the customer promise.

scenarios.given: a corridor payment that exceeds the destination system limit
scenarios.then: the payment is blocked with a clear limit message. the amount is not silently reduced or split without customer agreement

scenarios.given: the originating leg is confirmed but the destination confirmation is absent
scenarios.then: the payment enters the investigation state. the end-to-end status is not reported as Complete

questions.question: What is the FedNow maximum transaction value?
questions.explanation: FedNow has a maximum of USD 10 million, effective November 2025, with a participant default of USD 100,000.

questions.question: What is the RTP limit?
questions.explanation: The RTP limit is USD 10 million from 9 February 2025.

questions.question: What is the UPI limit for specified categories?
questions.explanation: The UPI limit is INR 5 lakh for specified categories from December 2024.

questions.question: Technical connectivity alone proves two instant systems are interoperable. True or false?
questions.explanation: False. Interoperability also needs alignment of scheme rules, limits, operating hours, finality and dispute processes.
